questions.question: Name two pharmacodynamic mechanisms that explain bacterial killing and differentiate antibacterial classes, giving two example antibiotics for each.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 pharmacodynamic mechanisms which explain bacterial killing and differentiate between antibacterial classes? Give two examples of antibiotics for each pharmacodynamic mechanism.

questions.model_answer: (1) Concentration-dependent killing: rate and extent of killing rise with the peak concentration (high peak/MIC or AUC/MIC), often with a prolonged post-antibiotic effect allowing extended dosing intervals - e.g. aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones (daptomycin also qualifies). (2) Time-dependent killing: efficacy depends on maintaining free drug above the MIC for a sufficient fraction of the dosing interval (fT>MIC), with little benefit from higher peaks - e.g. β-lactams (penicillins) and clindamycin/macrolides; optimized by prolonged or continuous infusion.
questions.beyond_mandell: These PD killing classifications are established antimicrobial pharmacodynamics, not covered in this chapter slice.

cohort_answer.text: Concentration-Dependent Killing: Aminoglycosides, Fluoroquinolones, Daptomycin - rate/extent of killing increases with peak drug concentration; AG and FQ also have post-antibiotic effect; can be given at longer dosing intervals than predicted by half-life. Time-Dependent Killing: all beta-lactams, Clindamycin, Macrolides - free concentration maintained above MIC for a drug-specific fraction of time between doses achieves efficacy; maximizing duration of exposure (continuous infusions) leads to greater efficacy. (Alternate answer - bacteriostatic vs bactericidal: Bacteriostatic - inhibit growth/division - Tetracycline, Linezolid, Macrolides, Clindamycin. Bactericidal - kills bacteria - all beta-lactams, TMP/SMX (sometimes), Glycopeptides (weakly), Fluoroquinolones, Aminoglycosides.)

cohort_answer.text: Renal function/CrCl; Drug monitoring: peak; Drug monitoring: trough. When gentamicin used in endocarditis for synergy with beta-lactam or vancomycin against enterococcus/staph/strep, use 3mg/kg in 2-3 divided daily doses, target peak 3-5mg/L and trough <1mg/L; ODD should not be used given lack of data in this context (S. viridans 3mg/kg/day). Note: high-level aminoglycoside resistance in enterococci mediated by aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes which eliminate synergistic bactericidal effect - should not use gentamicin for synergy in this context. Toxicity mechanisms: renal proximal tubular cells (internalization of aminoglycoside activates apoptotic pathway, subsequent necrosis of proximal tubule cells); Type 1 hair cells (target of vestibular toxicity - aminoglycosides penetrate endolymph, cochlear and vestibular tissue, apoptotic cell death in organ of Corti and vestibular apparatus). Non-biochemical monitoring: audiometry at baseline and monthly; electronystagmography; dynamic visual acuity testing for oscillopsia (loss of visual acuity of 3+ rows suggests vestibular dysfunction, prompting discontinuation and ENT referral); ototoxicity usually irreversible, can appear after treatment ends, cumulative risk with repeated exposure. Flaccid paralysis: neuromuscular blockade is rare but serious/potentially lethal, occurs when disease state or concomitant drug interferes with neuromuscular transmission (e.g. myasthenia gravis, infantile botulism, concomitant neuromuscular blocking agents, FQs, macrolides, Mg sulfate); blockade from inhibition of presynaptic ACh release and postsynaptic receptor blockade; treatment: stop aminoglycoside, consider calcium gluconate (most cases) or neostigmine (if also MG).

questions.model_answer:
a) All enterococci have intrinsic low-level resistance to aminoglycosides, so low-level results are not clinically meaningful; only high-level resistance (HLR) testing predicts whether the synergistic effect with a cell-wall agent is preserved.
b) High-level resistance to both gentamicin and streptomycin abolishes the synergistic bactericidal effect of an aminoglycoside combined with a beta-lactam (or vancomycin); the aminoglycoside can no longer be used for synergy, so a double beta-lactam regimen (ampicillin plus ceftriaxone) should be used instead.
c) Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes: HLR to gentamicin is mostly due to the bifunctional enzyme AAC(6′)-Ie-APH(2″)-Ia; HLR to streptomycin is due to 30S ribosomal subunit mutations or a streptomycin adenylyltransferase.

cohort_answer.text: Only high-level resistance reported: Don't report low-level resistance since all enterococci have intrinsic low-level resistance to aminoglycosides; loss of synergism with beta lactams/vanco if high-level AG resistance present. Therapeutic consequence: Can no longer use AG for synergy with beta-lactam/vanco against enterococcus, if used will lead to clinical failure/higher relapse. Mechanism: AG-modifying enzymes (N-acetylation, O-nucleotidylation, O-phosphorylation) alter the drug so it can no longer bind the 30s ribosome subunit.

questions.model_answer: a) Aminoglycoside killing is concentration-dependent: a single large daily dose maximizes peak/MIC (efficacy rises to ~90% at peak/MIC >8) and exploits the PAE, while saturable proximal-tubular uptake means once-daily dosing deposits less drug in the renal cortex, lowering/delaying nephrotoxicity. b) Piperacillin-tazobactam killing is time-dependent (T>MIC); continuous infusion keeps free drug above the (elevated) MIC for the whole interval, maximizing bacterial exposure. c) Vancomycin efficacy tracks 24-h AUC/MIC; more frequent (thrice-daily) dosing raises AUC/MIC to hit target for MRSA.

cohort_answer.text: Once-daily gentamicin rationale: Aminoglycoside bactericidal activity is concentration dependent - higher peak/MIC ratio gives greater rate/extent of kill; goal is to maximize drug concentration at site of infection (optimum when exposure is ~8-10x MIC). Aminoglycosides exhibit a post-antibiotic effect (PAE, 0.5-8hrs). Saturable uptake in renal tubule cell/inner ear - once daily dosing gives lower renal cortical tissue concentration than divided/continuous dosing. Adaptive resistance (first exposure effect) - down-regulation of uptake after initial exposure; longer dosing interval preserves antibacterial activity. Decreases emergence of resistant subpopulations when peak is ≥8x MIC. Continuous Pip-Tazo infusion: maintains drug levels above MIC longer (time-dependent killing), better for bugs with minimal PAE. Vancomycin TID vs BID: killing depends on 24hr AUC/MIC; more frequent dosing gives higher AUC/MIC and better killing. NB. Vancomycin is cleared renally so actual dosing depends on weight/CrCl; goal trough >15 in severe infections.

questions.model_answer: a) The post-antibiotic effect is the persistent suppression of bacterial growth that continues after short antimicrobial exposure once drug concentration has fallen below the MIC (a delay before the organism re-enters logarithmic growth); duration depends on the specific organism-drug combination, concentration, and exposure time. b) Aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones (both give a ~2-6 h PAE against gram-negative bacilli); carbapenems such as imipenem also produce a PAE against GNB, and beta-lactams generally show a PAE against gram-positive organisms.

cohort_answer.text: PAE = inhibition of bacterial growth following exposure to an antibiotic even after drug concentration falls below MIC, exhibited by delay before microorganisms re-enter log-growth in vitro. Possible mechanisms: nonlethal damage induced by the antimicrobial resulting in slow recovery; persistence of antimicrobial at bacterial binding sites (ribosomes, DNA gyrase) and periplasmic space. Specific microorganism-antimicrobial combination is most important factor influencing presence/duration of PAE, along with concentration and length of exposure. In human studies, aminoglycosides (extended PAE against GNB) effective with once-daily dosing. Classes exhibiting PAE: Aminoglycosides (PAE against GNB, lasts 2-6 hrs); Fluoroquinolones (PAE against GNB, lasts 2-6 hrs); beta-lactams generally do not exhibit PAE against GNB (except imipenem) but induce ~2hr PAE against GP organisms.

cohort_answer.text: a) Enterococcal endocarditis requires bactericidal regimen but beta-lactams alone aren't readily bactericidal; synergistic bactericidal effect achieved with aminoglycoside addition; synergism = >=2 log10 increase in killing at 24h compared to beta-lactam alone; gentamicin and streptomycin are the two compounds recommended; HLR defined by growth at 2000mg/L streptomycin and 500mg/L gentamicin on BHI agar (or 1000mg/L streptomycin in BHI broth); HLR to both abolishes synergistic effect; evaluation for HLR is standard of care for endovascular/severe enterococcal infections. b) Gentamicin can be used for synergy in endovascular infections. c) Aminoglycoside modifying enzyme (AME) - bifunctional AAC(6')-APH(2'')-Ia confers high level gentamicin resistance due to mutations in 30S ribosomal subunit.

questions.model_answer:
a) Aminoglycosides show concentration-dependent killing and a postantibiotic effect; high-dose once-daily dosing maximizes the peak/MIC and 24-hour AUC/MIC ratios (efficacy rises as peak/MIC exceeds 8-10) while the drug-free interval limits saturable proximal-tubular uptake, giving equal or better efficacy with less nephrotoxicity.
b) Beta-lactams show time-dependent killing, so efficacy depends on the time free concentration remains above the MIC (T>MIC); continuous infusion maximizes T>MIC for an organism with a borderline/intermediate MIC, whereas intermittent q6h dosing has troughs that fall below the MIC.
c) Vancomycin efficacy tracks the AUC/MIC ratio; more frequent (q8h) dosing achieves the target AUC with lower peaks, theoretically reducing toxicity while maintaining exposure.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the once-daily aminoglycoside principle is grounded in this chapter; the piperacillin-tazobactam (beta-lactam T>MIC) and vancomycin (AUC/MIC) pharmacodynamics come from general antimicrobial PK/PD, not the aminoglycoside chapter.

cohort_answer.text: a) Higher dose extended interval dosing of gentamicin achieves higher peak levels while avoiding toxic trough levels; potentially lower risk of nephrotoxicity based on animal studies (no difference in ototoxicity); post-antibiotic effect with ongoing killing after concentration drops below MIC; convenience of once daily dosing/monitoring; equivalent clinical efficacy. b) Continuous infusion: reduced mortality in meta-analysis (greater efficacy), also observed with prolonged infusion duration vs traditional dosing; can use lower total daily dose to maintain T>MIC. c) Shorter dosing interval (TID/q8h) allows target AUC/MIC to be achieved with lower loading doses, keeping peaks lower; theoretically reduces nephrotoxicity.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Rifampin - induces CYP3A4, decreasing tacrolimus levels (risk of rejection). (2) Clarithromycin - inhibits CYP3A4, increasing tacrolimus levels. (3) Fluconazole - inhibits CYP3A4, increasing tacrolimus levels.
b) (1) Gentamicin + tacrolimus - no true CYP-mediated interaction, but additive nephrotoxicity (both cause renal injury/acute kidney injury). (2) Mycophenolate mofetil + TMP-SMX - no true CYP interaction, but additive myelosuppression (leukopenia/cytopenias).
questions.beyond_mandell: Clarithromycin and fluconazole mechanisms and both additive-toxicity combinations are established pharmacology; the rifamycin chapter grounds only the rifampin-tacrolimus induction effect.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Serum creatinine / creatinine clearance. (2) Gentamicin peak concentration. (3) Gentamicin trough concentration.
b) (1) Hearing loss / tinnitus (cochlear). (2) Imbalance, nausea/vomiting or oscillopsia (vestibular).
c) (1) Renal proximal tubular cells. (2) Type I vestibular hair cells (and cochlear hair cells of the organ of Corti).
d) Audiometry / high-frequency audiogram (electronystagmography also acceptable).
e) Aminoglycoside-induced neuromuscular blockade, from inhibition of presynaptic acetylcholine release and postsynaptic receptor blockade. Management: stop the gentamicin, provide respiratory/supportive care, and administer IV calcium (calcium gluconate).
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter gives the mechanism of neuromuscular blockade but not the treatment; IV calcium (calcium gluconate) is established management.

cohort_answer.text: Lab tests: Creatinine; Gentamicin trough; Gentamicin peak. Non-biochemical test: Audiometry. Cell types affected: Vestibular type 1 hair cells; Renal proximal tubular cells. Flaccid paralysis cause: Gentamicin neuromuscular blockade. Treatment: IV calcium, supportive care
